That was a constant which included a proposal for an unconditional launch of political dialogue without delay, with a perspective of a political solution engendering essential autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija within Serbia without impinging on Serbia and Yugoslavia's territorial integrity and sovereignty. The second type of activities was aimed at using legitimate means to eliminate the threat of terrorism to resolve the consequences of terrorist conduct and terrorist activities, to prevent their reoccurrence, and thereby to contribute to a normalisation of the economic, social, and other forms of life in Kosovo and Metohija. Those were the two tracks which were concurrent. In both cases, the authorities, the institutions, did nothing to impede the possibility for the international factors and international community to grasp the situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you this: The measures undertaken in Kosovo and Metohija, were they directed against people who were not engaging in terrorism irrespective of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Serbia's policy and the strategy of Serbia and from Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was to prevent terrorism by means which can be used anywhere in the world to thwart terrorism or the threat of terrorism anywhere in the world, be it terrorism in the Near or Middle East, in Afghanistan or in Corsica or anywhere else. And by the same token, Serbia undertook measures to protect the state from clear evident separatist tendencies and terrorism being used as means to achieve political goals and ends. As has already been stated, apart from several resolutions of the UN Security Council, there have been no other calls on terrorists to cease their terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija. Calls were directed mainly at Serbia and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, while in the meantime calls by the Security Council to members of the UN were just dead letters on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. Let's please take a look at D160, Exhibit D160. That would be tab 12 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic. Let's take a look at page 2, please. Could you please comment, and acting pursuant to Chapter 7 of the Charter of the United Nations, that would be item 7.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As per paragraph of UN Security Council 1199, UN Security Council requests that all parties, groups, and individuals immediately cease hostilities and maintain a cease-fire in Kosovo which would enhance the prospects for a meaningful dialogue and the reduction -- and to reduce the risks of human catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please go back to paragraph 2 on this page, starting with "condemning all acts of violence," could you please comment that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here UN Security Council's call is reiterated, in other words, their condemnation was reiterated, condemnation of a practice which had been going for a long time, which had been incontestable by anybody, and that practice boiled down to allowing terrorists, a terrorist KLA, to be armed, funded, and trained. That was a practice which was uncontested and not for the first time the UN Security Council states that as a fact in one of their documents and calls on member states to desist or to make sure that it ceases. Your Honours, I would like to use one example as an illustration on the attitude of certain member states towards this obligation. I would like to cite the example of the United Kingdom. So the United Kingdom is a permanent member of the UN Security Council. Not only did they vote for this UN Security Council Resolution, but were one of the initiators and proponents of it. And, inter alia, this resolution contains a request which could be paraphrased as follows: No member of the UN Security Council or no member of the UN should encourage in any way the conflicts in Kosovo, neither through funding, arming, or training. And when the UK representative voted for this UN Security Resolution 1199, at the same time Mr. Paddy Ashdown visited the camps of the terrorist KLA in Kosovo and Metohija - we have video footage of that - and practically encouraged that terrorist organisation to persist with their commitments. He inspected their weapons. He asked them how did they get those weapons, which route it took, and he said, "Be mindful and be careful so that the other side does not get information that you possess those weapons." Your Honours, I must be serious and honourable here, but I must say that this is political hypocrisy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The Court will hand down their determination. Let's deal with the facts here in your examination. Could we please focus on paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an important position of the Security Council because finally they had accepted the -- Serbia and Yugoslavia's position that meaningful political dialogue should be started without imposition of any conditions with strict dead-lines. That would mean that this represents support, in my opinion and to the best of my knowledge, to the initiatives launched by Serbia, supported by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to launch political dialogue without delay and without preconditions on a peaceful political solution, with due respect being paid to the equal rights of all ethnic minorities and communities and all individuals in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Could we move on to page 3, please, and could you tell us briefly under 5(b).

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: By decision of the Security Council, the Milosevic-Yeltsin statement of June 1998 is being accepted as a part of the positions of the Security Council. And in this part of the resolution, the agreement between Milosevic and Yeltsin is being re-affirmed. Under (b) it is stated that no repressive actions against the peaceful population may be carried out. I wish to point out that the official policy of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the struggle against terrorism and the protection of the civilian population. And I wish to recall the fact that the terrorist KLA in my conviction was not an armed force in the sense of an army; it was a terrorist organisation which here and there had uniformed individuals and groups, but very frequently there were terrorists who carried out terrorist acts wearing civilian clothes. A policy was resolutely against any kind of violence towards the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, do you know whether repressive measures were ever undertaken against the peaceful civilian population in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Though this area is within the terms of reference of other departments, as the minister for foreign affairs, I never had information on use of force against the peaceful civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like you to look at item (c) regarding the freedom of movement. Does this apply to the period from the beginning of the summer, or is this something new?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were never any problems for foreign diplomatic representatives even before the Kosovo Diplomatic Mission was formed to travel and stay in Kosovo and Metohija, to contact any entities, be they state entities or civilian bodies. So this is just a statement which was given I think primarily out of caution and in expectation of a broader international presence in Kosovo and Metohija so that personnel of international organisations and diplomatic missions should be safe, and they were. During my term of office, there wasn't a single case of violence or any serious incident in respect of foreign diplomatic representatives. Yugoslavia fully respected the Vienna Convention on diplomatic immunity for foreign diplomatic representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at page 4 and tell me briefly under item 6, it is pointed out that the leadership of Kosovo Albanians should condemn all terrorist activities. Was this requirement observed by the leadership of the Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This requirement was never met, and that is not the whole problem because no one undertook any steps or measures on a bilateral level to oblige representatives of the Albanians, both the political representatives and the terrorist wings, to condemn terrorism. The political representatives of the Albanian national minority never condemned publicly the terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, and they were never identified in the Security Council for not observing this obligation. And this was the discrepancy with respect to the treatment of the other side, if I may put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look briefly at items 7 and 11. Were these prohibitions implemented after this resolution was adopted?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said items 7 and 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are calls on the members of the United Nations by the Security Council addressed in accordance with Chapter 7 of the UN Charter, according to which member states of the world organisation in accordance with their own legislation should prevent the financing, arming, and training of terrorists. And this obligation was never fulfilled, and except for being repeated from one resolution to the next, there were no practical concrete steps taken to see it implemented. The consequence of this was the continued influx of arms, the accumulation of funds, the most sophisticated electronic and other equipment for military use, and uncontrolled escalation of terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you inform us regarding the security situation in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia at the end of September and beginning of October 1998.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that in the summer of 1998 the state launched an anti-terrorist campaign to suppress terrorism and to normalise the social, economic, and other activities in Kosovo and Metohija. At the end of September, 1998, Kosovo again had a system of unified authority throughout the territory, public services were functioning, the local government bodies which had been disenfranchised in the territory held by the terrorist KLA resumed their activities and in many places a local police force was formed from the local inhabitants to keep the law and order so that in that period terrorist activities were halted and social and economic life and in Kosovo and Metohija normalised to a maximum degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you tell us when talking about the authority established at the end of September and beginning of October, which authorities do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the official authorities and the authority of local governments which had been prevented from functioning in parts of Kosovo and Metohija that were controlled by the terrorist KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware of the response of NATO and its members?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The reactions were to criticise Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, accusing them that in resorting to these measures excessive force had been used. I think there was a lack of necessary understanding for a legitimate defence of state institutions and for the establishment of a unified system that would be functional throughout the territory of Serbia. This criticism was also a reflection of the bias on the part of a segment of the international community with respect to the separatist forces and the terrorist organisation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any danger of an armed conflict or a unilateral attack on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were threats by NATO representatives addressed at the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and if I am not mistaken, at the beginning of October 1999 [as interpreted] NATO adopted an Act. Order in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was this Act. Order a unilateral NATO act, or was it under the auspices of the UN and Security Council?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This Act. Order was adopted without consultation with the United Nations and without the approval of the Security Council, which is the only body authorised for questions of peace and security in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small correction, page 53, line 14, "October 1998" it should say instead of "1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, how did the international political situation develop further at the beginning of October 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as Kosovo and Metohija is concerned, I can say that the terrorist activities were reduced to such an extent that they almost entirely stopped --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. I'm not referring to the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, but I'm talking about the development of the political situation in the direction of dealing with the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija and in the context of this NATO Act. Order.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia remained dedicated to their platform of peaceful political settlement and the initiation of a political dialogue without preconditions and without delay. This strategic policy never changed for a moment, regardless of all pressure --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I'd like us to see a document, 9008-4296 [as interpreted], 65 ter 972-6. Mr. Jovanovic, this is a document of the 5th of October, conclusions of the joint chamber, of the chamber of citizens, and the chamber of republics of the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These conclusions of the Federal Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of the 5th of October in essence meant a confirmation of the strategy of a peaceful political settlement which had been adopted by the Republic of Serbia. And the implementation of a unified concept of a peaceful political settlement on the basis of clear principles evident from the documents of the Republic of Serbia were now adopted and reinforced at the level of the federal state, and those principles are: Dialogue, territorial integrity of Serbia and Yugoslavia, solutions on autonomy in accordance with international standards and in conformity with the constitutions of Serbia and Yugoslavia, the equality of all national communities and all citizens in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00466.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would suggest that we have our technical break now because we will be moving on to a new set of interesting documents, so I think it would be better not to interrupt later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- Mr. Djurdjic, with a view to resuming just before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at tab 14, Mr. Jovanovic, and D008-4318 in e-court, and 65 ter of the Defence 976 -- correction, 978 -- 976, 65 ter document 976 -- I apologise, 978, my mistake. Yes, that's the document. Mr. Jovanovic, here we have a document by the federal government dated the 14th of October, 1998, proposed agenda on the draft agreement between the federal government and the OSCE. But before we start working on that document, could you please tell us - that would be tab 14 in your binder - could you please tell us were there any talks preceding the signing of that agreement between you and Mr. Geremek at the political level and who was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were talks by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, and representatives of the US administration, Mr. Richard Holbrooke. These talks took place over two or three days, and they ended on the 13th of October, 1998 in Belgrade. During those negotiations, an agreement was reached on the 13th of October labelled in the media as the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you present during those negotiations between Milosevic and Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not take part in those talks because at the same time I took part at the south-east Europe summit at Antalya. A head of the Yugoslav delegation was the president of the federal government, Momir Bulatovic. I was a member of that delegation in my capacity as minister of foreign affairs, and there was some other members of the delegation. So at that time I was not in Belgrade, I was in Antalya.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that Milosevic and Holbrooke reached that agreement. When you say that, our first association would be a written document. To the best of your knowledge, what was the form of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Finesse, I did not say agreement, I said an arrangement. I'm not sure what the term will be in translation. An agreement is a formal, signed document; an arrangement may not be signed document but it can be. It can retain its political character and it can rely on bona fide carrying out on the parts of the parties to the arrangement. I am familiar with the positions that were agreed upon within that arrangement and later on I will testify that the Serbian government accepted those positions. But in my work I did not have occasion to see any signed, formal agreement on those matters. As I said, it was a political arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Let's take this document and in the briefest possible terms as per that agenda could you tell us -- and in keeping with the manner in which foreign policy was conducted -- could you please expound on this document, familiarise us with it.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: So an arrangement had been reached by the president of the federal republic, Mr. Milosevic, and representative of the international community, US envoy, Mr. Richard Holbrooke, on the 13th of October. As I already stated, foreign policy is within the remit of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but other actors within the political system and other institutions take part in creating that foreign policy, in keeping with their constitutional powers. And within that system it was not enough to reach an agreement on matters. It was necessary for the federal government to accept such arrangements or agreements because the federal government was in charge of foreign policy. And here we have an invitation to the members of the federal government and an agenda is attached to it, and we'll later see that that agreement will be later on adopted as the position of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00467.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab number 15 for your benefit, Mr. Jovanovic. That would be D008-4320 in e-court and the 65 ter number 979. Mr. Jovanovic, you're about to be shown a document by the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs dated 14th October 1998. Could you please comment it briefly.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a coded circular memo issued by the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs to Yugoslav diplomatic representative offices abroad, whereby those diplomatic representation offices are notified that they had received en clair federal government's communique on the adoption of the agreement between Yugoslavia and OSCE on the verification mission's establishment in Kosovo and Metohija, and those diplomatic representative offices are hereby instructed to hand over at the appropriate level this communique to the representatives of the countries they are accredited to. There are particular notes for New York mission, Vienna, Strasbourg, and the Geneva mission, depending on the specific tasks of each particular mission as being very important in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00468.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now please could we take a look at Exhibit P835. That will be tab 16 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic. But before that I would like to ask you this: Who was your interlocutor, or who was the other party in this agreement and what was their position?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement on the verification mission of Kosovo and Metohija I signed on behalf of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; on the part of the OSCE this document was signed by Bronislaw Geremek, the then-foreign minister of Poland and then chair of the OSCE in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at Roman numeral I, item 1. Let's hear your comments on that.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a part concerning the establishment of the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission as a mission of the OSCE. It discusses that in principle mission will be valid for one year, to be extended either at the initiative of the OSCE or at the initiative of the Yugoslav side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is important to note here, as been heard in previous testimony, that before that verification mission we had had the KDOM, Kosovo Diplomatic Missions, and this document discusses that KDOM being upgraded and transformed into the Kosovo Verification Mission. Another important paragraph is item 6 under Roman numeral I, which lays down the obligation of the FRY government to guarantee the safety and security of the Kosovo Verification Mission and all its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your knowledge, pursuant to item 5 of this document, did the OSCE take over the missions and tasks of the KDOM, and did KDOM end up as part of the verification mission?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: For a while, for a long while, KDOM ran and functioned in parallel with the Kosovo Verification Mission. There were problems in certain degree of slowness in setting up the Kosovo Verification Mission. There were problems which in no way were connected with the Yugoslav side because the establishment of the Kosovo Verification Mission depended primarily on the goodwill and the readiness of member states to delegate their representatives to the Kosovo Verification Mission. From the establishment until its end, the KVM never surpassed the 1200-member mark, although the agreement envisaged that they number 2.000 and even more if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try to analyse items 6 and 8.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already stated, this agreement envisaged that only the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be to guarantee the security of the mission and all its members. It was not only due to the fact that it was established and envisaged so in this agreement, but also because in item 8 it is stated that the members of the verification mission will enjoy the diplomatic status in terms of the Vienna Convention and it will enjoy the privileges and immunities conferred by such status, which means that all members of the KVM were guaranteed immunity and entitlements pursuant to the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations by the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at item 1 under Roman numeral II.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this provision it is envisaged that there -- the tasks of the mission was to be to verify whether all parties in Kosovo comply with council -- UN Security Council Resolution 1199 and that the KVM is to report instances of progress to both the OSCE Permanent Council in Vienna and to the United Nations Security Council in New York, but from the viewpoint of the interest of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where I held the position of federal minister, an important provision was this envisaging the obligation of the KVM to send all reports submitted to the Permanent Council of the OSCE and the United Nations Security Council, to send those at the same time to the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, did the OSCE honour this obligation, and did they send those reports to the Yugoslav authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Although the mission was slow to be set up, they from the very beginning sent their initial reports to the addressees specified herein, but from its first steps until it withdrew on the 20th of March, 1999, that mission submitted to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia no written reports. Simply, they did not honour this reporting obligation as established by the presiding person of the OSCE, Mr. Geremek, by his signature on the agreement that I co-signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In this period from the establishment of the mission until they left the Federal Republic, did you take steps to obtain these reports and did you send such requests; and if so, to whom?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, both through the offices in Belgrade where the Kosovo Verification Mission had an office for liaising with the federal government and the foreign ministry, also through the staff of the verification mission in Pristina we did request that we be provided with these reports and we expressed our dissatisfaction because of the failure to comply with the signed obligation. Nevertheless, we never received even any explanation, there could be no justification, nor did we receive a single report from the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now look at Roman numeral III, special terms of reference, item 1?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this item headed by the words "special terms of reference," it is envisaged that the mission would travel throughout Kosovo to verify whether a cease-fire was being observed, that the mission would investigate reports of cease-fire violations, and that the mission would have freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. This provision on the freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo, what did it mean?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This meant that freedom of movement and access should not be disputed, and in my view, it is quite clear. The verification mission in Kosovo and Metohija was of a civilian nature, and this follows from the agreement. Its security was guaranteed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it had freedom of movement, which meant that they could visit any part of Kosovo and Metohija, that is, throughout Kosovo and Metohija and access means that they could go to certain locations, settlements, and that there would be no restrictions or problems with respect to the freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have heard during the proceedings here various interpretations of the freedom of movement and access by representatives of the Kosovo Verification Mission, but I'm interested in something else. Did you officially as the government of Yugoslavia or the foreign minister receive any formal protest against any limitation on the freedom of movement and access from members of the verification commission?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The ministry never received a formal protest from the verification mission in Kosovo and Metohija because of any possible violation of this obligation of freedom of movement and access. I know that there were different interpretations of this provision; however, freedom of movement and access should not be confused with inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in something else when dealing with this issue. First of all, who was authorised to interpret the agreement should there be any differences in the implementation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Provisions on the right of interpretation were not contained in the agreement itself. In that case, the parties' signatories could interpret the contents of various provisions, but sometimes interpretation is necessary and it is assumed that it would be done bona fide, but an interpretation cannot change the signed provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But since you and Mr. Geremek as the chairman signed this agreement in this period during the stay of the verification mission, did the two of you ever discuss different interpretations of individual provisions of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that what you said is important, the more so as only the signatories by their agreement and through mutual contacts can by agreement provide co-ordinated interpretation of what they signed. There's no one above the signatories who could interpret the contents of these provisions. Throughout the mandate of the verification commission, no protest, no request, no intervention did I receive from Minister Bronislaw Geremek as a signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And during the mission stay in Kosovo and Metohija, did you receive any request from the OSCE for a revision of the agreement or a revision of any provisions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No such requests were addressed in formal terms, in writing, or orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please look at item 4 and the end of it, the end of that paragraph, regarding the question of border control. Could you say a few words about that.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This provision envisages that the verification mission at the invitation of bodies of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or upon its own request will visit units for border control and accompanying them as they perform their normal border control duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this provision envisage the obligation for the verification mission to submit a request to do this; and if there is no such request, that it can do so only upon the invitation of the Federal Republic of Serbia's [as interpreted] authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you now look at Roman numeral IV, item 1.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this segment defines the composition and facilities. Heading the verification mission is the director, the mission director. It is assumed that he is responsible -- accountable for his work to the chairman of the OSCE. The next item envisages, as I have mentioned, that the mission will consist of 2.000 unarmed verifiers, and as I have already noted this figure was never achieved. The maximum number was about 1200 verifiers. There is here also the possibility envisaged that in addition to these 2.000 verifiers and assistants, the mission may engage experts for various areas. This provision was never referred to because the basic number of 2.000 verifiers was never achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. It says here, 2.000 unarmed verifiers. Could you tell me first, by profession these verifiers, mission members, what were they by profession?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the spirit of the agreement and all the arrangements made, this was a civilian mission of a diplomatic nature and enjoying diplomatic treatment and immunity in accordance with the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations. Therefore, it is clear that it was necessary to observe the civilian and diplomatic character of the mission. However, in view of the difficulty in filling in the required number, in practice the personnel that had previously performed certain duties in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia or elsewhere moved to Kosovo and Metohija as part of this verification mission. I know that within the mission there were many profession soldiers, either active-duty or retired soldiers, military and police experts who were in civilian clothes but there were colonels, generals, and other lower-ranking officers who were members of this diplomatic mission. So there was a certain discrepancy. The Yugoslav side as a signatory of the agreement did not expect this to be transformed partly into a mission of military, police, and other specialists, but that in good faith it would preserve its diplomatic and civilian nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell us what was the principal role of this civilian verification mission?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the negotiations and the document signed, this should have been the personification of neutrality and objectivity in reflecting the real situation, the real problems, and the real processes in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And according to Roman III, item 1, I see that it is noted that verification had to be carried out of the observation of cease-fires, that was a specific duty.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This does not change the civilian and diplomatic character of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in that context I wanted to ask you whether this formulation of the mandate, does it have anything to do with control of armaments and military facilities and equipment?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a military expert. For 40 years I have been a professional diplomat, but in my view arms control is the duty of inspection and not of verifiers of cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And since you're signatory of this agreement, was its intention verification and not inspection?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. That is how the agreement is called, on the establishment of a verification mission. There is no grounds for inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your own diplomatic experience, what is the difference between verification and inspection?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I can be fully qualified to give you the etymology of the words inspection and verification, but when talking about verification in the way it was conceived by the authors of this agreement, it is quite clear what its mandate, what its goals and methods were. As for inspection, in my conviction, inspection is the subject of separate agreements, protocols, and specialist arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. We shall now look at a document within the framework of this topic. D008-4186 and e-court tab 17 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic, and 65 ter it is 954. Mr. Jovanovic, we have here an agreement on subregional arms control signed in Florence, and as far as I can remember the Resolution 1160 refers to it, which was passed in March. So to come back to this agreement, did it envisage arms control in the territory of the signatory countries, and which were the signatories of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, every agreement of this kind on arms control establishes its own mechanism for implementation and inspection. By this agreement, the proportions of arms were established which Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Croatia were allowed to have, and this agreement is accompanied by a separate protocol on inspection. This is a very specific form of activity and mandate that can be entrusted to military experts only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Bearing in mind that provision of Resolution 1160, which refers to this agreement and all the countries' signatories of this agreement, was it possible for each of the parties' signatory of this agreement during the term of office of the Kosovo Verification Mission to carry out arms control throughout the territory of the Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could on the basis of the Security Council Resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But for the transcript will you tell us who the signatories were.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the document itself we see Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republika Srpska, then as witnesses representatives of France, Germany, the Russian Federation, Italy, the United Kingdom, and the United States of America; in other words, all members of the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00469.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at D008-4325, please. That would be 65 ter document 981.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Or tab 18 in your binder, Mr. Jovanovic. Please, very briefly, could you offer this -- your comments to this document.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The genesis of the agreement on the arrival of the verification mission was first item, the arrangement between Milosevic and Holbrooke; secondly, consent of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for the minister of foreign affairs to sign that document; the third stage was the signing of the agreement; and the fourth stage was the delivery of the signed agreement which had become part of the legal system of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to all ministries having specific tasks and obligations to carry it out. This document discusses the delivery of a legal document to departments who have duties to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D00470.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now if we could please take a look at D388, Exhibit D388 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, this is a decision on the establishment of the federal government's mission for co-operation with the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission that would be dated 16th of May [as interpreted], 1998. Could you please briefly say what's the mandate of this commission and what would be its position within the framework of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Departing from the fact that the signed agreement envisages for different departments of the federal government to become involved, this document shows that a commission is being established with a basic task to co-ordinate different departments and services within the government on the task of implementing the agreement concluded with the OSCE. So this is a document that is adopted only seven days after the agreement on the verification mission had been signed, which means that this document was adopted practically before the OSCE mission was set up in Kosovo and Metohija. Let me construe this as an illustration of the federal government's attitude towards an international obligation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could they report to and who were they responsible to?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the federal government who established it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see it's 19th of October, 1998, that is the date, and your agreement was signed on the 16th, so it's three days?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Quickly one document, Y009-1917 -- 0907. That would be 1128 on the 65 ter list. And on Prosecution's 65 ter list is 4013. Briefly, Mr. Jovanovic, could you please tell us what is the federal government's decision on the 29th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a decision is on including two additional members to the federal commission, Loncar and Mr. Jankovic, justice minister of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first document. Were you a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the government's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is time for us to adjourn, but I do -- before that move to tender this document into evidence, the last one, and the previous one is Exhibit D388, the one dated 19th. And the supplement is dated 29th of October and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The supplement will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be D00471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Are you saying that concludes your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For today, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know it's time. How much longer should we expect, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to be misguiding in my estimates, but what awaits us are documents which can be briefly tendered very fast. I would like to familiarise you with a failure of mine, an omission of mine, and to apologise to Mr. Stamp. I did not react in time and to notify you that our next witness is not going to be Mr. Andric but Mr. Gojovic, Radomir Gojovic, and I believe that I have failed to notify the Bench of that fact. He's the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't understand clearly what you were saying about the time that you need to complete your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Your Honour, that another session will be sufficient for me to tender the document -- the remaining documents -- with the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must adjourn now for today. We resume tomorrow at 2.15. And if there is any assistance needed by Mr. Jovanovic about arrangements overnight, an officer will be available for that purpose. We adjourn until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of January, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
